Remove learned frame-rate baselines from Sonic adaptive quality

Following the screen, the goal stays 60 FPS (the screen rate if slower);
a fixed cap remains its own goal. Learning the original tier's stable
cadence lowered visible detail while frames were still smooth (e.g.
120 -> 80 FPS on a 240 Hz screen), and Sonic's load rises with the music,
so a cadence learned in an intro reads as a drop in every chorus.

Durable preference storage, the confirmed one-time quality reset and the
early end of an ineffective-lowering pause on new load are kept. The help
text, README and notes describe the fixed goal again; the baseline tests
are replaced by a controller check of the 120 -> 80 FPS case.

Persist manual quality, explicit disable and upgrade markers in app-owned desktop storage. Detect high-refresh slowdowns against measured stable cadence and allow changed or severe load to break ineffective-lowering backoff. Verify with targeted regressions and real desktop restarts across localhost origins.

Reset automatically chosen quality tiers to ultra once on upgrade

2.4.0 defaulted to low and 2.4.1 picked medium/low by GPU; neither was
the user's choice, and with adaptive quality on by default they would cap
Sonic WE detail. On the first run, a non-ultra tier without a recorded
manual choice becomes ultra, once. It saves through the quality buttons'
path so the on-disk copy cannot restore the old tier, is not counted as
a manual choice, and retries if later scripts are not loaded yet.

2.4.0 did not record manual choices, so a tier picked then is also reset.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Turn Sonic adaptive quality on by default with a 60 FPS goal, stutter detection and effectiveness checks

Default-on and manual adaptation share one rule. The goal is 60 FPS when
following the screen (the screen rate if slower) or the user's fixed cap,
at every tier: missing a high refresh rate is no longer frame loss.

The meter also counts long frames (over 2.5 goal intervals); 6 of the last
8 seconds with 2+ long frames is reported as stutter even when average FPS
is fine. Each lowering is checked by the next report: if neither FPS rose
10% nor long frames fell 30%, it is undone and lowering pauses 5 minutes,
doubling to 20, since detail was not the bottleneck.

Users who never refused adaptation are switched on; a manual switch-off or
the 2.4.1 keep-current choice stays respected. Sonic's opt-in and GPU
advice cards are removed; the first automatic lowering per run says where
to switch it off. The ordinary-scene GPU tier tip is unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Back off repeated restore probes and use the display's reported refresh rate

Failed restore probes now double their wait (1, 2, 4, 8, then 10 min max)
instead of retrying every minute; a success or new target resets it. In a
30-minute step-load simulation this cuts time below 80% from about 270s to
78s with the same average detail.

Sonic's FPS goal now comes from Electron's displayFrequency, passed with
the window state. The rAF-gap estimate swung between 48 and 240 Hz while
Sonic WE drew in its iframe, resetting drop evidence each time. It stays
as the fallback.

The adaptive UI smoke test now sends the configured loss threshold, admits
only its controlled reports and waits until the controller is eligible.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Fix Sonic drop detection and restore quality with small probes

Align frame-loss evidence with the effective FPS goal and clear recovery history when that goal changes. Replace long tier lockouts with bounded small recovery probes and rollback, preserving topography animation state and releasing instance GPU buffers.

Keep the quality notice above the bottom bar, stop restore flapping and follow the screen rate

The floating notice now sits 12px above the bottom bar's resting edge.
A restore that brings load back within 30s blocks that tier for 10 min,
doubling up to an hour. Tiers no longer cap FPS: frame rate follows the
foreground FPS setting; under follow-screen the top tier may drop one
step to chase high refresh, lower tiers only drop below 60 FPS.

Frame drops are judged from 1s buckets after a 3s warmup: four slow

With adaptive quality on, lowering no longer waits a 20s cooldown and
very slow frames drop two tiers; restores stay slow and back off when
they bring load back. Closing the notice only snoozes it for this run.
Ordinary scenes on integrated/software renderers get a one-time offer
